blocks.body:
At a party of six people, some pairs know each other and some do not. However the acquaintances are arranged, there are always three people who all know each other or three who are mutual strangers. With five people this can fail. Ramsey theory is the study of statements of this shape: once a structure is large enough, any way of splitting it into a few classes leaves one class containing a large orderly piece.

The basic question is quantitative: how many vertices force a one-coloured complete subgraph of a given size? The answer, the Ramsey number, is known exactly only in a handful of small cases, and its growth rate is a central open problem of combinatorics.

blocks.title: The party problem
blocks.body:
Translate the party into a graph: six vertices, every pair joined by an edge, the edge red if the two people know each other and blue otherwise. This is a 2-colouring of the edges of the complete graph $K_6$ (see [[graph-basics]]). We want a monochromatic triangle: three vertices whose three connecting edges have the same colour.

Pick any vertex $v$. It has five edges, so by [[pigeonhole]] at least three of them share a colour, say red, going to $a$, $b$, $c$. If any of the edges $ab$, $bc$, $ca$ is red, it forms a red triangle with $v$. If none is red, then $abc$ is a blue triangle. Either way we are done.

Five vertices are not enough. Place them at the corners of a regular pentagon, colour the five sides red and the five diagonals blue. The red edges form a 5-cycle, which has no triangle, and the blue edges form another 5-cycle (the pentagram), which has no triangle either.

So six is the exact threshold. The general question asks the same thing with triangles replaced by larger complete graphs, and with possibly different targets for the two colours.

blocks.title: Ramsey number
blocks.body:
For integers $k, \ell \ge 1$, the Ramsey number $R(k,\ell)$ is the least $n$ such that every colouring of the edges of $K_n$ in red and blue contains a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_\ell$. The diagonal case is written $R(k) = R(k,k)$.

Equivalently, thinking of the red edges as a graph $G$: every graph on $R(k,\ell)$ vertices contains a clique of size $k$ or an independent set of size $\ell$, and some graph on $R(k,\ell)-1$ vertices contains neither. The party problem says $R(3,3) = 6$.

blocks.title: Why the numbers exist
blocks.body:
It is not obvious that $R(k,\ell)$ is finite: perhaps for some $k$ there are arbitrarily large colourings with no monochromatic $K_k$. The argument for triangles generalises, and it gives a recursive bound.

Small cases first. A single vertex is a $K_1$ of either colour, so $R(1,\ell) = R(k,1) = 1$. For $R(2,\ell)$: if any edge is red we have a red $K_2$; otherwise everything is blue, so $\ell$ vertices suffice and $\ell - 1$ do not (colour all edges blue). Hence $R(2,\ell) = \ell$, and by symmetry $R(k,2) = k$. Swapping the colours shows $R(k,\ell) = R(\ell,k)$ in general.

blocks.title: Ramsey's theorem with the Erdős–Szekeres bound
blocks.body:
For all $k, \ell \ge 2$,
$$R(k,\ell) \le R(k-1,\ell) + R(k,\ell-1).$$
Consequently $R(k,\ell)$ is finite for all $k,\ell \ge 1$ and
$$R(k,\ell) \le \binom{k+\ell-2}{k-1}, \qquad\text{in particular}\qquad R(k) \le \binom{2k-2}{k-1} < 4^{k}.$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Assume $R(k-1,\ell)$ and $R(k,\ell-1)$ are finite, and let $n = R(k-1,\ell) + R(k,\ell-1)$. Take any red/blue colouring of $K_n$ and a vertex $v$. The other $n-1$ vertices split into the set $A$ of those joined to $v$ by a red edge and the set $B$ of those joined by a blue edge. Since $|A| + |B| = n - 1$, we cannot have both $|A| \le R(k-1,\ell) - 1$ and $|B| \le R(k,\ell-1) - 1$, because then $|A|+|B| \le n-2$. So one of the following holds.

1. $|A| \ge R(k-1,\ell)$. Inside $A$ there is a red $K_{k-1}$ or a blue $K_\ell$. A blue $K_\ell$ finishes the proof; a red $K_{k-1}$ together with $v$ is a red $K_k$, since all edges from $v$ to $A$ are red.
2. $|B| \ge R(k,\ell-1)$. Inside $B$ there is a red $K_k$, which finishes the proof, or a blue $K_{\ell-1}$, which together with $v$ is a blue $K_\ell$.

This proves the recursive inequality, and finiteness follows by induction on $k+\ell$ from the base cases $R(1,\ell) = R(k,1) = 1$.

For the binomial bound, also induct on $k+\ell$. The bound holds when $k=1$ or $\ell=1$, because $\binom{\ell-1}{0} = \binom{k-1}{k-1} = 1$. For $k,\ell \ge 2$, the recursion and the induction hypothesis give
$$R(k,\ell) \le \binom{k+\ell-3}{k-2} + \binom{k+\ell-3}{k-1} = \binom{k+\ell-2}{k-1}$$
by Pascal's rule. Finally $\binom{2k-2}{k-1}$ is one term of $\sum_j \binom{2k-2}{j} = 4^{k-1}$, so it is less than $4^k$.

blocks.title: Small values and the growth of R(k)
blocks.body:
The recursion gives $R(3,3) \le R(2,3) + R(3,2) = 6$, which is exact. Exact values are known only for a few small pairs. Three facts worth knowing:

- $R(3,4) = 9$ (see the second example below).
- $R(4,4) = 18$, proved by Greenwood and Gleason in 1955. The lower bound comes from the Paley graph on 17 vertices: join $i$ and $j$ in $\mathbb{Z}/17$ when $i - j$ is a nonzero square modulo 17. This graph has no clique and no independent set of size 4.
- $R(5,5)$ is unknown. It is known that $43 \le R(5,5) \le 46$: the lower bound is Exoo's colouring of $K_{42}$ (1989), and the upper bound is a large computer-assisted argument of Angeltveit and McKay (2024).

For general $k$ the bounds are exponential with different bases. In 1947 Erdős proved $R(k) > 2^{k/2}$ for all $k \ge 3$ by showing that a uniformly random colouring of $K_n$ with $n = \lfloor 2^{k/2} \rfloor$ has, with positive probability, no monochromatic $K_k$. This argument is the subject of [[probabilistic-method]]. Together:
$$2^{k/2} < R(k) \le 4^{k} \qquad (k \ge 3).$$
(The inequality $\sqrt{2}^{\,k} \le R(k)$ also holds for $k = 2$, where $R(2) = 2$, but not for $k = 1$, where $R(1) = 1$.)

Since 1947 the base $\sqrt2$ in the lower bound has not been improved, only constant factors in front. For the upper bound, Conlon (2009) improved $\binom{2k-2}{k-1}$ by a factor that grows faster than any power of $k$, but the base 4 stood until 2023, when Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe proved
$$R(k) \le (4-\varepsilon)^k$$
for a fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ and all large $k$. This was the first exponential improvement over the 1935 bound of Erdős and Szekeres. Whether $\lim R(k)^{1/k}$ exists, and what it is, remains open.

The lower bound is not constructive: random colourings work, but no explicit colouring of $K_n$ is known whose largest monochromatic clique is as small as a random one's, of order $\log n$.

blocks.title: More colours and larger subsets
blocks.body:
The same argument works with $r$ colours. Let $R_r(k)$ be the least $n$ such that every $r$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$. Picking a vertex $v$ and splitting the other vertices by the colour of their edge to $v$ shows by induction that $R_r(k)$ is finite. For triangles with three colours the answer is $R_3(3) = 17$, also due to Greenwood and Gleason. Their lower-bound colouring of $K_{16}$ uses the field with 16 elements: colour the edge $\{x,y\}$ according to which coset of the subgroup of cubes contains $x - y$.

Edges are 2-element subsets. Ramsey's original 1930 theorem, proved as a lemma in a paper on decision problems in logic, colours $m$-element subsets.

blocks.title: Ramsey's theorem (finite form)
blocks.body: For all positive integers $m$, $r$ and $k$ there is an $N$ such that, however the $m$-element subsets of an $N$-element set are coloured with $r$ colours, there is a $k$-element subset all of whose $m$-element subsets have the same colour.

blocks.title: The general philosophy
blocks.body:
The general theorem is proved by induction on $m$, using the case $m - 1$ as the graph case used single vertices. Its bounds grow like towers of exponentials, and for $m \ge 3$ the true growth is still not understood (see [[hypergraphs]]).

Many results share this structure: colour a large object, find a structured monochromatic piece. Schur's theorem (monochromatic solutions of $x + y = z$) follows directly from the graph case, as the third example shows. Van der Waerden's theorem on monochromatic arithmetic progressions needs a different proof (see [[ramsey-arithmetic]]). The infinite version, that every colouring of the pairs of an infinite set has an infinite monochromatic subset, is the starting point of [[infinite-combinatorics]].

blocks.title: At least two monochromatic triangles
blocks.body: Show that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_6$ contains at least two monochromatic triangles.
blocks.solution:
Call a pair of edges at a common vertex a bichromatic angle if the two edges have different colours. If vertex $v$ has $r_v$ red edges and $5 - r_v$ blue edges, it is the apex of $r_v(5 - r_v)$ bichromatic angles. Since $r_v \in \{0,\dots,5\}$, this is at most $2 \cdot 3 = 6$.

A monochromatic triangle has no bichromatic angles. A triangle that is not monochromatic has two edges of one colour and one of the other, so exactly two of its three angles are bichromatic. Every bichromatic angle lies in exactly one triangle, the one obtained by closing it up. Hence
$$2 \cdot \#\{\text{non-monochromatic triangles}\} = \sum_v r_v(5 - r_v) \le 6 \cdot 6 = 36.$$
So at most 18 of the $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ triangles are non-monochromatic, and at least 2 are monochromatic.

The bound is sharp. Split the six vertices into two groups of three, colour edges inside a group red and edges between the groups blue. The two groups are red triangles; there is no blue triangle, since the blue graph is bipartite.

blocks.title: Computing R(3,4)
blocks.solution:
The recursion gives $R(3,4) \le R(2,4) + R(3,3) = 4 + 6 = 10$. We improve this by one using parity.

Suppose the edges of $K_9$ are coloured with no red triangle and no blue $K_4$. Fix a vertex $v$, let $A$ be its red neighbours and $B$ its blue neighbours, so $|A| + |B| = 8$.

- Inside $A$ there is no red edge, since such an edge together with $v$ would be a red triangle. So $A$ spans only blue edges, and as there is no blue $K_4$, $|A| \le 3$.
- Inside $B$ there is no blue triangle, since with $v$ it would give a blue $K_4$. There is also no red triangle. As $R(3,3) = 6$, $|B| \le 5$.

Since $|A| + |B| = 8$, both bounds are attained: every vertex has exactly 3 red edges. Then the red graph has $9 \cdot 3 / 2$ edges, which is not an integer. This contradiction shows $R(3,4) \le 9$.

For the lower bound, colour $K_8$ on vertices $\mathbb{Z}/8$ by making $\{i,j\}$ red when $i - j \equiv \pm 1$ or $4 \pmod 8$. A red triangle would need three differences from $\{\pm1, 4\}$ that add up to $0 \pmod 8$, and no such combination exists. Checking the 70 four-element subsets (or arguing by hand) shows that each contains a red edge, so there is no blue $K_4$. Hence $R(3,4) > 8$.

blocks.title: Schur's theorem from Ramsey's theorem
blocks.body: Show that for every $r$ there is an $N$ such that, however $\{1, 2, \dots, N\}$ is coloured with $r$ colours, there are $x, y, z$ of the same colour with $x + y = z$ ($x = y$ is allowed). For $r = 2$, find the least such $N$.
blocks.solution:
Let $N = R_r(3) - 1$ and fix a colouring $\chi$ of $\{1,\dots,N\}$. Colour the edges of the complete graph on vertices $\{0, 1, \dots, N\}$ by giving the edge $\{i, j\}$ the colour $\chi(|i - j|)$. This graph has $R_r(3)$ vertices, so it has a monochromatic triangle $a < b < c$. Put $x = b - a$, $y = c - b$, $z = c - a$. These three numbers lie in $\{1,\dots,N\}$, have the same colour, and satisfy $x + y = z$.

For two colours this gives $N = R(3,3) - 1 = 5$. It is the least possible: colour $1$ and $4$ red, $2$ and $3$ blue. The red sums $1+1$, $1+4$, $4+4$ equal $2$, $5$, $8$, none red; the blue sums $2+2$, $2+3$, $3+3$ equal $4$, $5$, $6$, none blue. So four numbers can be coloured with no monochromatic solution, while five cannot.

blocks.body:
- A monochromatic $K_k$ means all $\binom{k}{2}$ edges among the $k$ chosen vertices have one colour. It is not enough for the edges along a path or a cycle through them to agree.
- $R(k,\ell)$ is a threshold for every colouring. To prove $R(k,\ell) > n$ you must exhibit one colouring of $K_n$ (or prove one exists); to prove $R(k,\ell) \le n$ you must handle all colourings.
- The binomial bound is not exact in general: it gives $R(4,4) \le 20$, while the truth is 18.
- Ramsey's theorem finds a monochromatic substructure, not a large colour class. Questions about how many edges force a $K_k$, whatever their colour, belong to Turán's theorem (see [[extremal-graphs]]), which has quite different answers.

- [[probabilistic-method]]: Erdős's lower bound for $R(k)$ is the founding example of proving existence by random choice.
- [[ramsey-arithmetic]]: Schur, van der Waerden and Rado colour integers and look for monochromatic solutions of equations or arithmetic progressions.
- [[infinite-combinatorics]]: the infinite Ramsey theorem and partition relations for cardinals, some of them independent of the usual axioms.
- [[hypergraphs]]: Ramsey numbers for colourings of triples grow much faster and are far less understood.
- [[discrete-geometry]]: the Erdős–Szekeres theorem on convex polygons follows from Ramsey's theorem for 4-element subsets.
- [[extremal-graphs]] and [[graph-coloring]]: related forcing questions where density, not colouring, is the hypothesis.

1. Use the recursion to show $R(3,5) \le 14$.
2. Prove that $R_3(3) \le 17$: every 3-colouring of the edges of $K_{17}$ has a monochromatic triangle.
3. Show that for $k, \ell \ge 2$, if $R(k-1,\ell)$ and $R(k,\ell-1)$ are both even, then $R(k,\ell) \le R(k-1,\ell) + R(k,\ell-1) - 1$.
4. Prove that every 2-colouring of the edges of $K_7$ contains at least four monochromatic triangles, by adapting the angle-counting argument for $K_6$.

sources.ref: Campos, Griffiths, Morris & Sahasrabudhe, An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey (2023)
